Diabetes Warriors (#WeAreNotWaiting)

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Citizen scientists hack their way to cutting edge diabetes treatment

Unique Selling Point:
They call themselves Loopers. They go by the hashtag #WeAreNotWaiting. They're an international community joined by social media and open-source innovation, and they're creating the medical solutions they are tired of waiting for big tech companies to provide.

Summary:
Type 1 Diabetes is an auto-immune disease. At worst, it causes coma and death - at best, it means a lifetime of blood sugar monitoring, insulin injections and meal planning. It's increasingly diagnosed in children under 5, who are too young to check their own blood sugar levels or respond to dangerous lows or highs. This is a problem for parents, who wake up constantly every night to check levels, then send the child to school where they can't keep an eye on them. Medical technology helps: insulin pumps which constantly inject pre-programmed amounts of insulin into the bloodstream, and continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) which track blood sugar every five minutes, but is still lacking. The first CGMs sent data to a receiver that had to stay within range of the monitor, so when a child was at school, their data was unavailable to anyone not nearby.
A growing band of tech-savvy parents has spent years working on their own solutions. John Costik created Nightscout, hacking his son's CGM to transmit its data to the cloud where he could access it from anywhere. And adult T1D Dana Lewis created the ultimate diabetes tech: she hacked her insulin pump, creating an algorithm that would respond on its own to unexpected or predicted highs and lows, adjusting the insulin delivery without Dana having to intervene. This is called closing the loop.
These innovators have made all their programming and design available open-source online, so people around the world are using it. In South Africa, Jaco Cronje installed and improved Nightscout for himself, and has helped less tech-savvy people with theirs. 18 year-old Chloe Royston closed the loop on her own pump, which she says is allowing her to study overseas this year, away from her parents' watchful eyes.
And finally tech companies are responding, bringing out CGMs that can be linked to an app, and last year, the first ever FDA-approved closed-loop artificial pancreas.

Further information:
The major difference between a non-hacked pump attached to a sensor, and a closed-loop system, is that the pump will not respond on its own to the data coming from the sensor. A base rate of insulin delivery is calculated with the help of an endocrinologist, based on the patient's unique data, and this is programmed into the pump. If the diabetic knows s/he is going to have a large meal or go to the gym later, s/he must then 'bolus' (imcrease delivery) or pause it to avoid an unpleasant high or low. The closed loop does this on its own, predicting micro highs and lows minute by minute as well as over long periods, using AI programming, and adjusting the insulin delivery accordingly.
The new FDA approved artificial pancreas system (APS) that was approved last year is a different system. It has two pumps, one containting insulin which lowers blood sugar, and one containing glucagon, which raises it. This is much closer to what a healthy pancreas does, responding to lows and highs by increasing delivery of one hormone or the other into the blood stream. Even the hacked pumps can only pause or reduce the insulin delivery. But the new APS will be extremely expensive, not least because glucagon could not be stored for more than 24 hours until recently.
Blood sugar lows are dangerous because they can make a diabetic fall into a coma and die if they are not assisted quickly. As a result, most diabetics tend to run their blood sugar deliberately slightly high to avoid this risk. However, high blood sugar has serious longterm consequences including nerve damage, kidney damage and blindness. The closed loop allows diabetics to run their blood sugar much lower because the controls are so much finer, avoiding those risks.
Worldwide, diabetes kills more people every year that HIV, TB and malaria combined. In South Africa, as often happens, we have no idea of how many people suffer from diabetes. In state healthcare, diabetes treatment is still extremely basic, relying on multiple daily injections with a pre-mixed insulin solution. This means there is no flexibility in diet or activity: the patient must eat and exercise according to the insulin delivered, not the other way round. Of course, many patients don't do this and experience poor health due to poor management. Apparently Thembisa Hospital has an excellent programme, however - we could visit there to counter the high-tech element and see how low-tech solutions can work. Some state hospitals are finalising tenders to being pilot projects offering insulin pumps to patients.
We also have the possibility of interviewing Kerry Kalweit who is a T1D and is studying medicine to become an endocrinologist. She runs an NGO called Youth With Diabetes and is currently introducing a pilot project to get all SA state patients with diabetes onto a national patient registry. There is also an ongoing issue of discrimination in schools (including well-resourced private schools) against children with diabetes. Teachers do not want to have to deal with potential low blood sugar situations and some children have actually been turned away, unconstitutionally. Kerry's group also negotiates with and trains schools on this basis.
There are many other projects looking into other cures for T1D including cell replacement therapy and a bionic replacement pancreas. Some patients do receive pancreas transplants but these only last for about 5 years and in SA are only offered in conjunction with another essential transplant (eg kidneys).

Press Release:


Type 1 Diabetes management is an endless daily routine of blood glucose testing and insulin dosing. Unable to produce insulin, Type 1 Diabetics must inject it multiple times daily, or wear a pump which delivers a pre-programmed dose. Low blood sugar can be fatal; too high means long-term effects like kidney failure. A continuous glucose monitor can provide real-time blood sugar readings. But even for those who can plug into a high-tech device, management of this potentially fatal disease is far from perfect. That's why a worldwide movement of tech-savvy patients connected under the hashtag #wearenotwaiting is hacking its own way to relieving some of this burden.

Script:


VO1: Every month, Saif-Ali Moosa visits the Charlotte Maxeke diabetes clinic. He has Type 1 Diabetes, an auto-immune disease causing the body to attack its own insulin-producing cells.
UPSOUND: Saif-Ali Moosa: It’s like a tiger you know, in a circus. You have to first learn to get used to it, tame it. And once you tame it and take control of it, you’re the boss.
LINK: Like the vast majority of diabetics in South Africa, Saif manages his potentially fatal chronic condition with a daily regimen of injections, finger-prick blood sugar tests, and carb counting.
UPSOUND: Saif-Ali Moosa: At first I ran away, the nurses had to catch me. I put on a good fight. But as the years went by I started injecting by myself.
VO2: Over 400 million people worldwide are living with diabetes. Around 5% of those have Type 1 Diabetes, says endocrinologist, Dr David Segal.
UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: what is it like for a day in the life of someone that’s got Type 1 Diabetes?
Dr Segal: So you wake up in the morning hoping you didn’t have a bad night and your blood sugar is within target range. Because if you’re high you wake up tired and thirsty and irritable and brain fog. If you’re low you’ve usually got a headache or had restless sleep.
VO3: Unable to produce insulin, Type 1 Diabetics must inject it multiple times daily, or wear a pump which delivers a pre-programmed dose. Low blood sugar can be fatal; too high means long-term effects like kidney failure. A continuous glucose monitor can provide real-time blood sugar readings.
LINK: In South Africa, state patients still don’t have access to this technology. But even for those who can plug into a high-tech device, diabetes management is far from perfect.
VO4: Early monitors transmitted only to a short-range receiver, so parents couldn’t monitor their diabetic children at school. And even with a pump, diabetics have to adjust their insulin dose dozens of times daily. New technologies take years to reach the market. So tech-savvy patients took matters into their own hands.
UPSOUND: Jaco Cronje: We are not waiting for the big competitor companies to work together or for the regulators to regulate the system or for the design companies to innovate. We can do it ourselves and we can do it faster than them.
VO4: Computer engineer Jaco Cronje was diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes at 27. Seeking ways to help manage his condition, he found a worldwide movement connected under the hashtag WeAreNotWaiting.
UPSOUND: Jaco Cronje: It was started by a dad who had a child with T1D and he wanted to remotely monitor his child.
VO5: John Costik started Nightscout when he created software to transmit readings from his 4 year-old son’s monitor to the cloud. He made the code available open source online, allowing diabetics worldwide to use and modify it for themselves. Jaco did just that – then began to help others.
UPSOUND: Jaco Cronje: This is the device I make. You need to carry it around with you. So I use TicTac sweeties.
UPSOUND: Vicky Santana: It comes in a TicTac box so you don’t know, does it really work?
Macfarlane Moleli: What’s this MacGyver stuff?
Vicky Santana: Ja, really MacGyver!
VO6: Vicky Santana’s son Valentino was diagnosed weeks before his first birthday. Although on insulin, he had four seizures due to uncontrolled blood sugar before Vicky met Jaco, who built a TicTac box receiver to send data from Valentino’s monitor to a phone he carries around his waist, and to Vicky’s smart watch.
UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: You’re like Dr Gadget. Do you have games on that phone of yours?
Valentino Santana: No. Mom deleted them.
Vicky Santana: I did. I did.
VO7: Valentino now has a newer monitor and doesn’t need to carry the TicTac box, but Vicky still uses Nightscout to monitor his levels.
UPSOUND: Vicky Santana: My husband and I both wear watches so we can go out now. During the days if it’s holidays or on the weekends he wakes up, gets dressed and he’s gone. As long as he’s got his phone I can monitor and I’m happy.
VO8: Mainstream companies have started to offer similar apps. But there are still advantages to community driven innovation, not least the lower cost.
UPSOUND: Jaco Cronje: The big companies is catching up. But the community is always a step ahead.
LINK: Hacking a monitor is one thing, but what if your pump could act like a real pancreas, responding to your blood sugar levels automatically and then adjusting your insulin without you having to even touch it? This is the holy grail of diabetes management: closing the loop.
UPSOUND: Dr Segal: Closing the loop is the ability to take the human being out of the equation.
UPSOUND: Dana Lewis: It wasn’t the fact that we closed the loop that was novel. It was way that we did it as a group of patients sharing our knowledge.
VO9: Dana Lewis embarked on diabetes DIY looking for a way to make the alerts on her glucose monitor louder. She found a ‘hacker’ willing to share his code and so began OpenAPS, which closed the loop over three years before a similar system became commercially available.
UPSOUND: Dana Lewis: We don’t have to spend so much time doing the job that a computer can do, because a computer can absolutely do it better.
VO10: OpenAPS picks up data from the monitor, runs it through an algorithm and instructs the pump to increase or reduce the insulin feed every five minutes. And the software is constantly evolving.
UPSOUND: Dana Lewis: We’re able to really focus on one problem at a time, and not worry about the fact that we can’t solve everything, we can’t cure diabetes.
VO11: Like Nightscout, all OpenAPS coding is available open source online – and accessible to at least one enterprising local teenager.
UPSOUND: Chloe Royston: I was probably checking my sensor every 20 minutes to half an hour and making a different decision on whether to have more insulin or more food. So that took up a lot of my day.
VO12: Chloe Royston was diagnosed when she was 7. She’s used an insulin pump most of her life. When she was accepted to Harvard University, she started looking for ways to manage her diabetes overseas without her parents’ supervision.
UPSOUND: Chloe Royston: I originally didn’t think that I would be able to do it so I kind of put it aside for the year but towards the end of matric I decided to look at it more again. The day after finals I finished the system so I could start using it so that was exciting.
VO13: Despite her lack of experience with computer programming it took just a few weeks for Chloe to programme her own computer board and link her monitor and pump.
UPSOUND: Chloe Royston: Even though you physically have to do it yourself you’re not doing it alone because everyone is there to help you and troubleshoot any issues that you have. The closed loop system has definitely allowed me to go overseas now and also allowed me and my parents to feel more comfortable with me going.
VO14: Closing the loop has helped Chloe manage diabetes as a competitive golfer. And it’s inspired her to consider a degree in computer science at Harvard.
UPSOUND: Chloe Royston: I hadn’t considered computer programming or technology as a career to go into. So this has really opened my eyes to a whole other area that I can help people.
UPSOUND: Dr Segal: What you’ve got is highly motivated individuals who know a lot about their own condition.
Macfarlane Moleli: When you look at your diabetes hackers, it’s a very tiny proportion of the population of people that actually have it.
Dr Segal: That’s I think the only criticism you can have. This is not generalizable. The technologies are ridiculously expensive and we’ve got people dying from no access to insulin.
VO15: High-tech healthcare remains largely out of reach for patients like Saif. But social media and smart devices have fuelled a much wider movement towards self-driven medicine.
In Sweden, Sara Riggare uses fitness devices and her own app to track her Parkinson’s disease.
UK engineer Tal Golesworthy designed the Exovasc to repair the aortic dilation caused by his Marfan Syndrome. Over 140 patients have since received one.
And the 3D printed “robo hand” designed by South African Richard van As is now used by amputees worldwide.
UPSOUND: Dana Lewis: It’s about changing the paradigm between being a passive recipient of healthcare and saying I’m going to take things in my own hands. It’s not diabetes alone. It’s any patient who says I don’t want to wait. And I don’t have to because I found a way by myself or in partnership with my community to make our lives better today.


10 SECOND PROMO
VO: Living with Type 1 diabetes involves constant maintenance. But some maverick patients are hacking their own solutions to manage this potentially fatal disease.

15 SECOND PROMO
UPSOUND: Dr David Segal: test, inject, look at what you’re going to eat, monitor the response. And then you get to do the whole thing again the next day.
VO: Managing type 1 diabetes requires non-stop maintenance, which is why some tech-savvy patients have hacked their way to peace of mind.

15 SECOND PROMO
UPSOUND: Dana Lewis [22:06:28] It’s about changing the paradigm between being a passive recipient of healthcare and saying I’m not going to wait.
VO: Patient-driven healthcare is a growing trend, and Type 1 diabetics are designing their own ways to manage this lifelong disease.

30 SECOND PROMO
UPSOUND: Chloe Royston: I was probably checking my sensor every 20 minutes to half an hour and making a different decision on whether to have more insulin or more food. Even when you’re not actually doing anything, it’s always at the back of your mind.
VO: Type 1 Diabetes management is an endless daily routine of blood glucose testing and insulin dosing. But a worldwide movement of tech-savvy patients is hacking its own way to relieving some of this burden.
UPSOUND: Dana Lewis: we don’t have to spend so much time doing the job that a computer can do, because a computer can absolutely do it better.

HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 21 September 2018 Press Release: Type 1 Diabetes management is an endless daily routine of blood glucose testing and insulin dosing. Unable to produce insulin, Type 1 Diabetics must inject it multiple times daily, or wear a pump which delivers a pre-programmed dose. Low blood sugar can be fatal; too high means long-term effects like kidney failure. A continuous glucose monitor can provide real-time blood sugar readings. But even for those who can plug into a high-tech device, management of this potentially fatal disease is far from perfect. That's why a worldwide movement of tech-savvy patients connected under the hashtag #wearenotwaiting is hacking its own way to relieving some of this burden. Script: VO1: Every month, Saif-Ali Moosa visits the Charlotte Maxeke diabetes clinic. He has Type 1 Diabetes, an auto-immune disease causing the body to attack its own insulin-producing cells. UPSOUND: Saif-Ali Moosa: It’s like a tiger you know, in a circus. You have to first learn to get used to it, tame it. And once you tame it and take control of it, you’re the boss. LINK: Like the vast majority of diabetics in South Africa, Saif manages his potentially fatal chronic condition with a daily regimen of injections, finger-prick blood sugar tests, and carb counting. UPSOUND: Saif-Ali Moosa: At first I ran away, the nurses had to catch me. I put on a good fight. But as the years went by I started injecting by myself. VO2: Over 400 million people worldwide are living with diabetes. Around 5% of those have Type 1 Diabetes, says endocrinologist, Dr David Segal. UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: what is it like for a day in the life of someone that’s got Type 1 Diabetes? Dr Segal: So you wake up in the morning hoping you didn’t have a bad night and your blood sugar is within target range. Because if you’re high you wake up tired and thirsty and irritable and brain fog. If you’re low you’ve usually got a headache or had restless sleep. VO3: Unable to produce insulin, Type 1 Diabetics must inject it multiple times daily, or wear a pump which delivers a pre-programmed dose. Low blood sugar can be fatal; too high means long-term effects like kidney failure. A continuous glucose monitor can provide real-time blood sugar readings. LINK: In South Africa, state patients still don’t have access to this technology. But even for those who can plug into a high-tech device, diabetes management is far from perfect. VO4: Early monitors transmitted only to a short-range receiver, so parents couldn’t monitor their diabetic children at school. And even with a pump, diabetics have to adjust their insulin dose dozens of times daily. New technologies take years to reach the market. So tech-savvy patients took matters into their own hands. UPSOUND: Jaco Cronje: We are not waiting for the big competitor companies to work together or for the regulators to regulate the system or for the design companies to innovate. We can do it ourselves and we can do it faster than them. VO4: Computer engineer Jaco Cronje was diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes at 27. Seeking ways to help manage his condition, he found a worldwide movement connected under the hashtag WeAreNotWaiting. UPSOUND: Jaco Cronje: It was started by a dad who had a child with T1D and he wanted to remotely monitor his child. VO5: John Costik started Nightscout when he created software to transmit readings from his 4 year-old son’s monitor to the cloud. He made the code available open source online, allowing diabetics worldwide to use and modify it for themselves. Jaco did just that – then began to help others. UPSOUND: Jaco Cronje: This is the device I make. You need to carry it around with you. So I use TicTac sweeties. UPSOUND: Vicky Santana: It comes in a TicTac box so you don’t know, does it really work? Macfarlane Moleli: What’s this MacGyver stuff? Vicky Santana: Ja, really MacGyver! VO6: Vicky Santana’s son Valentino was diagnosed weeks before his first birthday. Although on insulin, he had four seizures due to uncontrolled blood sugar before Vicky met Jaco, who built a TicTac box receiver to send data from Valentino’s monitor to a phone he carries around his waist, and to Vicky’s smart watch. UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: You’re like Dr Gadget. Do you have games on that phone of yours? Valentino Santana: No. Mom deleted them. Vicky Santana: I did. I did. VO7: Valentino now has a newer monitor and doesn’t need to carry the TicTac box, but Vicky still uses Nightscout to monitor his levels. UPSOUND: Vicky Santana: My husband and I both wear watches so we can go out now. During the days if it’s holidays or on the weekends he wakes up, gets dressed and he’s gone. As long as he’s got his phone I can monitor and I’m happy. VO8: Mainstream companies have started to offer similar apps. But there are still advantages to community driven innovation, not least the lower cost. UPSOUND: Jaco Cronje: The big companies is catching up. But the community is always a step ahead. LINK: Hacking a monitor is one thing, but what if your pump could act like a real pancreas, responding to your blood sugar levels automatically and then adjusting your insulin without you having to even touch it? This is the holy grail of diabetes management: closing the loop. UPSOUND: Dr Segal: Closing the loop is the ability to take the human being out of the equation. UPSOUND: Dana Lewis: It wasn’t the fact that we closed the loop that was novel. It was way that we did it as a group of patients sharing our knowledge. VO9: Dana Lewis embarked on diabetes DIY looking for a way to make the alerts on her glucose monitor louder. She found a ‘hacker’ willing to share his code and so began OpenAPS, which closed the loop over three years before a similar system became commercially available. UPSOUND: Dana Lewis: We don’t have to spend so much time doing the job that a computer can do, because a computer can absolutely do it better. VO10: OpenAPS picks up data from the monitor, runs it through an algorithm and instructs the pump to increase or reduce the insulin feed every five minutes. And the software is constantly evolving. UPSOUND: Dana Lewis: We’re able to really focus on one problem at a time, and not worry about the fact that we can’t solve everything, we can’t cure diabetes. VO11: Like Nightscout, all OpenAPS coding is available open source online – and accessible to at least one enterprising local teenager. UPSOUND: Chloe Royston: I was probably checking my sensor every 20 minutes to half an hour and making a different decision on whether to have more insulin or more food. So that took up a lot of my day. VO12: Chloe Royston was diagnosed when she was 7. She’s used an insulin pump most of her life. When she was accepted to Harvard University, she started looking for ways to manage her diabetes overseas without her parents’ supervision. UPSOUND: Chloe Royston: I originally didn’t think that I would be able to do it so I kind of put it aside for the year but towards the end of matric I decided to look at it more again. The day after finals I finished the system so I could start using it so that was exciting. VO13: Despite her lack of experience with computer programming it took just a few weeks for Chloe to programme her own computer board and link her monitor and pump. UPSOUND: Chloe Royston: Even though you physically have to do it yourself you’re not doing it alone because everyone is there to help you and troubleshoot any issues that you have. The closed loop system has definitely allowed me to go overseas now and also allowed me and my parents to feel more comfortable with me going. VO14: Closing the loop has helped Chloe manage diabetes as a competitive golfer. And it’s inspired her to consider a degree in computer science at Harvard. UPSOUND: Chloe Royston: I hadn’t considered computer programming or technology as a career to go into. So this has really opened my eyes to a whole other area that I can help people. UPSOUND: Dr Segal: What you’ve got is highly motivated individuals who know a lot about their own condition. Macfarlane Moleli: When you look at your diabetes hackers, it’s a very tiny proportion of the population of people that actually have it. Dr Segal: That’s I think the only criticism you can have. This is not generalizable. The technologies are ridiculously expensive and we’ve got people dying from no access to insulin. VO15: High-tech healthcare remains largely out of reach for patients like Saif. But social media and smart devices have fuelled a much wider movement towards self-driven medicine. In Sweden, Sara Riggare uses fitness devices and her own app to track her Parkinson’s disease. UK engineer Tal Golesworthy designed the Exovasc to repair the aortic dilation caused by his Marfan Syndrome. Over 140 patients have since received one. And the 3D printed “robo hand” designed by South African Richard van As is now used by amputees worldwide. UPSOUND: Dana Lewis: It’s about changing the paradigm between being a passive recipient of healthcare and saying I’m going to take things in my own hands. It’s not diabetes alone. It’s any patient who says I don’t want to wait. And I don’t have to because I found a way by myself or in partnership with my community to make our lives better today. 10 SECOND PROMO VO: Living with Type 1 diabetes involves constant maintenance. But some maverick patients are hacking their own solutions to manage this potentially fatal disease. 15 SECOND PROMO UPSOUND: Dr David Segal: test, inject, look at what you’re going to eat, monitor the response. And then you get to do the whole thing again the next day. VO: Managing type 1 diabetes requires non-stop maintenance, which is why some tech-savvy patients have hacked their way to peace of mind. 15 SECOND PROMO UPSOUND: Dana Lewis [22:06:28] It’s about changing the paradigm between being a passive recipient of healthcare and saying I’m not going to wait. VO: Patient-driven healthcare is a growing trend, and Type 1 diabetics are designing their own ways to manage this lifelong disease. 30 SECOND PROMO UPSOUND: Chloe Royston: I was probably checking my sensor every 20 minutes to half an hour and making a different decision on whether to have more insulin or more food. Even when you’re not actually doing anything, it’s always at the back of your mind. VO: Type 1 Diabetes management is an endless daily routine of blood glucose testing and insulin dosing. But a worldwide movement of tech-savvy patients is hacking its own way to relieving some of this burden. UPSOUND: Dana Lewis: we don’t have to spend so much time doing the job that a computer can do, because a computer can absolutely do it better.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Citizen scientists hack their way to cutting edge diabetes treatment
metadata.Unique Selling Point: They call themselves Loopers. They go by the hashtag #WeAreNotWaiting. They're an international community joined by social media and open-source innovation, and they're creating the medical solutions they are tired of waiting for big tech companies to provide.
metadata.Summary: Type 1 Diabetes is an auto-immune disease. At worst, it causes coma and death - at best, it means a lifetime of blood sugar monitoring, insulin injections and meal planning. It's increasingly diagnosed in children under 5, who are too young to check their own blood sugar levels or respond to dangerous lows or highs. This is a problem for parents, who wake up constantly every night to check levels, then send the child to school where they can't keep an eye on them. Medical technology helps: insulin pumps which constantly inject pre-programmed amounts of insulin into the bloodstream, and continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) which track blood sugar every five minutes, but is still lacking. The first CGMs sent data to a receiver that had to stay within range of the monitor, so when a child was at school, their data was unavailable to anyone not nearby. A growing band of tech-savvy parents has spent years working on their own solutions. John Costik created Nightscout, hacking his son's CGM to transmit its data to the cloud where he could access it from anywhere. And adult T1D Dana Lewis created the ultimate diabetes tech: she hacked her insulin pump, creating an algorithm that would respond on its own to unexpected or predicted highs and lows, adjusting the insulin delivery without Dana having to intervene. This is called closing the loop. These innovators have made all their programming and design available open-source online, so people around the world are using it. In South Africa, Jaco Cronje installed and improved Nightscout for himself, and has helped less tech-savvy people with theirs. 18 year-old Chloe Royston closed the loop on her own pump, which she says is allowing her to study overseas this year, away from her parents' watchful eyes. And finally tech companies are responding, bringing out CGMs that can be linked to an app, and last year, the first ever FDA-approved closed-loop artificial pancreas.
metadata.Further information: The major difference between a non-hacked pump attached to a sensor, and a closed-loop system, is that the pump will not respond on its own to the data coming from the sensor. A base rate of insulin delivery is calculated with the help of an endocrinologist, based on the patient's unique data, and this is programmed into the pump. If the diabetic knows s/he is going to have a large meal or go to the gym later, s/he must then 'bolus' (imcrease delivery) or pause it to avoid an unpleasant high or low. The closed loop does this on its own, predicting micro highs and lows minute by minute as well as over long periods, using AI programming, and adjusting the insulin delivery accordingly. The new FDA approved artificial pancreas system (APS) that was approved last year is a different system. It has two pumps, one containting insulin which lowers blood sugar, and one containing glucagon, which raises it. This is much closer to what a healthy pancreas does, responding to lows and highs by increasing delivery of one hormone or the other into the blood stream. Even the hacked pumps can only pause or reduce the insulin delivery. But the new APS will be extremely expensive, not least because glucagon could not be stored for more than 24 hours until recently. Blood sugar lows are dangerous because they can make a diabetic fall into a coma and die if they are not assisted quickly. As a result, most diabetics tend to run their blood sugar deliberately slightly high to avoid this risk. However, high blood sugar has serious longterm consequences including nerve damage, kidney damage and blindness. The closed loop allows diabetics to run their blood sugar much lower because the controls are so much finer, avoiding those risks. Worldwide, diabetes kills more people every year that HIV, TB and malaria combined. In South Africa, as often happens, we have no idea of how many people suffer from diabetes. In state healthcare, diabetes treatment is still extremely basic, relying on multiple daily injections with a pre-mixed insulin solution. This means there is no flexibility in diet or activity: the patient must eat and exercise according to the insulin delivered, not the other way round. Of course, many patients don't do this and experience poor health due to poor management. Apparently Thembisa Hospital has an excellent programme, however - we could visit there to counter the high-tech element and see how low-tech solutions can work. Some state hospitals are finalising tenders to being pilot projects offering insulin pumps to patients. We also have the possibility of interviewing Kerry Kalweit who is a T1D and is studying medicine to become an endocrinologist. She runs an NGO called Youth With Diabetes and is currently introducing a pilot project to get all SA state patients with diabetes onto a national patient registry. There is also an ongoing issue of discrimination in schools (including well-resourced private schools) against children with diabetes. Teachers do not want to have to deal with potential low blood sugar situations and some children have actually been turned away, unconstitutionally. Kerry's group also negotiates with and trains schools on this basis. There are many other projects looking into other cures for T1D including cell replacement therapy and a bionic replacement pancreas. Some patients do receive pancreas transplants but these only last for about 5 years and in SA are only offered in conjunction with another essential transplant (eg kidneys).
